actions.justification: Mandatory action. Patient has hypertension and diabetes — both are major risk factors for AKI. This assessment is critical to identify predisposing conditions and guide further workup.
Mandatory action. Decreased urine output is the chief complaint; continuous monitoring of urine output is essential for AKI diagnosis and staging (KDIGO criteria: <0.5 mL/kg/h for >6h).
Mandatory action. Serum creatinine is the cornerstone of AKI diagnosis and staging per KDIGO guidelines. Baseline and serial creatinine values are needed to confirm AKI and determine severity.
Reassess vital signs to establish baseline and monitor for hemodynamic changes in the context of decreased urine output and AKI workup.
Decreased urine output in a patient with hypertension and diabetes requires assessment of volume status to differentiate pre-renal AKI from intrinsic or post-renal causes.
With creatinine already ordered, calculating AKI stage per KDIGO criteria will guide urgency and management of this patient's decreased urine output.
Calculate eGFR to accurately stage AKI/CKD and guide management decisions for this patient with decreased urine output, hypertension, and diabetes.

Review current medications for nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, metformin, contrast agents) that may be contributing to AKI and identify medications requiring dose adjustment given renal impairment.
Assess contrast-induced AKI risk, as this patient with diabetes and hypertension is at elevated risk if contrast imaging is being considered or was recently performed.

Patient with decreased urine output, hypertension, and diabetes with pending creatinine — nephrology consultation is warranted early to guide AKI workup and management, especially given high-risk comorbidities.

Patient has diabetes and hypertension and likely on medications (e.g., NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, metformin) that may be nephrotoxic or contraindicated in AKI — early discontinuation prevents further renal injury.
With suspected AKI and pending creatinine, contrast exposure should be avoided to prevent contrast-induced AKI in this high-risk diabetic/hypertensive patient.

Patient with decreased urine output and pending creatinine is at risk for hyperkalemia from AKI. ECG is warranted to screen for hyperkalemic changes (peaked T-waves, widened QRS) given renal impairment context.

With decreased urine output, hypertension, and diabetes as comorbidities, early assessment of renal replacement therapy need is prudent per KDIGO AKI guidelines to ensure timely intervention if indicated.

Given ongoing AKI workup with pending labs and high-risk comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes), nephrology input supports optimal management decisions regarding fluid strategy, medication adjustments, and RRT planning.
Patient has hypertension and diabetes — major risk factors for CKD. Assessing for underlying or developing CKD is critical to differentiate AKI from AKI-on-CKD and guide long-term management.
If RRT becomes necessary, early assessment of vascular access options (peripheral IV, central line, tunneled catheter) is important for timely intervention in AKI.
Formal evaluation of RRT indications (AEIOU criteria: Acidosis, Electrolytes, Intoxication, Overload, Uremia) is warranted given ongoing decreased urine output and AKI workup in progress.
NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and can worsen AKI by reducing renal perfusion; should be held in this patient with decreased urine output and pending creatinine.
Patient has diabetes and likely AKI; metformin should be held due to risk of lactic acidosis when renal function is impaired.
Early RRT planning is appropriate given AKI presentation with decreased urine output, especially with nephrology already consulted; ensures readiness if indications develop.

With decreased urine output and pending creatinine, identifying the etiology (prerenal, intrinsic, postrenal) is the critical next step to guide appropriate management in this hypertensive diabetic patient.
Patient has diabetes and hypertension with AKI - actively discontinuing any remaining nephrotoxic agents (beyond NSAIDs/metformin already held) is essential to prevent further kidney injury.
Patient should be informed of the AKI diagnosis, etiology workup findings, and the risk-benefit of upcoming treatment decisions including potential fluid administration or further interventions.
